claim: AANAT1 is expressed by Drosophila astrocytes in the adult brain.
source: We found that the enzyme arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase 1 (AANAT1) is expressed by Drosophila astrocytes and specific subsets of neurons in the adult brain.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, and it is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figures.

claim: AANAT1 is expressed by specific subsets of neurons in the adult brain.
source: We found that the enzyme arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase 1 (AANAT1) is expressed by Drosophila astrocytes and specific subsets of neurons in the adult brain.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, and it is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figures.

claim: AANAT1 acetylates monoamines and inactivates them.
source: AANAT1 acetylates monoamines and inactivates them, and we found that AANAT1 limited the accumulation of serotonin and dopamine in the brain upon sleep deprivation (SD).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro studies cited in the introduction (Hintermann et al., 1995) and by HPLC-MS data in the manuscript.

claim: AANAT1 limited the accumulation of serotonin and dopamine in the brain upon sleep deprivation.
source: AANAT1 acetylates monoamines and inactivates them, and we found that AANAT1 limited the accumulation of serotonin and dopamine in the brain upon sleep deprivation (SD).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-MS measurements showing increased serotonin and dopamine levels in AANAT1 mutant flies after sleep deprivation.

claim: Loss of AANAT1 from astrocytes caused flies to increase their daytime recovery sleep following overnight sleep deprivation.
source: Loss of AANAT1 from astrocytes, but not from neurons, caused flies to increase their daytime recovery sleep following overnight SD.
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data using cell-type specific RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Loss of AANAT1 from neurons did not cause flies to increase their daytime recovery sleep following overnight sleep deprivation.
source: Loss of AANAT1 from astrocytes, but not from neurons, caused flies to increase their daytime recovery sleep following overnight SD.
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data using neuron-specific RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: AANAT1 and astrocytes play a crucial role in the regulation of monoamine bioavailability and homeostatic sleep.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate a crucial role for AANAT1 and astrocytes in the regulation of monoamine bioavailability and homeostatic sleep.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sleep features are conserved among species.
source: Characteristic features of sleep are conserved among species (Pimentel et al., 2016), and from humans to insects sleep is influenced by neural circuits involving monoamines such as serotonin and dopamine (Nall and Sehgal, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pimentel et al., 2016.

claim: From humans to insects, sleep is influenced by neural circuits involving monoamines such as serotonin and dopamine.
source: Characteristic features of sleep are conserved among species (Pimentel et al., 2016), and from humans to insects sleep is influenced by neural circuits involving monoamines such as serotonin and dopamine (Nall and Sehgal, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nall and Sehgal, 2014.

claim: Glial cells take up and metabolize monoamines.
source: Glial cells are known to take up and metabolize monoamines (Inazu et al., 2003; Pelton et al., 1981; Suh and Jackson, 2007; Takeda et al., 2002) and they have been increasingly implicated in mechanisms of baseline and homeostatic sleep regulation in mammals and flies (Artiushin et al., 2018; Briggs et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2015; Clasadonte et al., 2017; Farca Luna et al., 2017; Frank, 2013; Gerstner et al., 2017; Halassa et al., 2007; Haydon, 2017; Pelluru et al., 2016; Seugnet et al., 2011; Stahl et al., 2018; Vanderheyden et al., 2018; Walkowicz et al., 2017), but it remains unknown whether and how glia might influence monoaminergic control of sleep.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Glial cells have been increasingly implicated in mechanisms of baseline and homeostatic sleep regulation in mammals and flies.
source: Glial cells are known to take up and metabolize monoamines (Inazu et al., 2003; Pelton et al., 1981; Suh and Jackson, 2007; Takeda et al., 2002) and they have been increasingly implicated in mechanisms of baseline and homeostatic sleep regulation in mammals and flies (Artiushin et al., 2018; Briggs et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2015; Clasadonte et al., 2017; Farca Luna et al., 2017; Frank, 2013; Gerstner et al., 2017; Halassa et al., 2007; Haydon, 2017; Pelluru et al., 2016; Seugnet et al., 2011; Stahl et al., 2018; Vanderheyden et al., 2018; Walkowicz et al., 2017), but it remains unknown whether and how glia might influence monoaminergic control of sleep.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: It remains unknown whether and how glia might influence monoaminergic control of sleep.
source: Glial cells are known to take up and metabolize monoamines (Inazu et al., 2003; Pelton et al., 1981; Suh and Jackson, 2007; Takeda et al., 2002) and they have been increasingly implicated in mechanisms of baseline and homeostatic sleep regulation in mammals and flies (Artiushin et al., 2018; Briggs et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2015; Clasadonte et al., 2017; Farca Luna et al., 2017; Frank, 2013; Gerstner et al., 2017; Halassa et al., 2007; Haydon, 2017; Pelluru et al., 2016; Seugnet et al., 2011; Stahl et al., 2018; Vanderheyden et al., 2018; Walkowicz et al., 2017), but it remains unknown whether and how glia might influence monoaminergic control of sleep.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Sleep is regulated by circadian clocks and a homeostatic drive to compensate for prolonged wakefulness.
source: Sleep is regulated by circadian clocks and a homeostatic drive to compensate for prolonged wakefulness, and growing evidence suggests that neural mechanisms controlling homeostatic sleep can be discriminated from those controlling baseline sleep (Artiushin and Sehgal, 2017; Donlea et al., 2017; Dubowy and Sehgal, 2017; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of sleep research.

claim: Neural mechanisms controlling homeostatic sleep can be discriminated from those controlling baseline sleep.
source: Sleep is regulated by circadian clocks and a homeostatic drive to compensate for prolonged wakefulness, and growing evidence suggests that neural mechanisms controlling homeostatic sleep can be discriminated from those controlling baseline sleep (Artiushin and Sehgal, 2017; Donlea et al., 2017; Dubowy and Sehgal, 2017; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: AANAT1lo mutants have normal baseline amounts of sleep and motor activity.
source: In Drosophila, mutants of arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase 1 (AANAT1lo) were reported to have normal baseline amounts of sleep and motor activity, but increased recovery sleep ('rebound') following deprivation (Shaw et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shaw et al., 2000.

claim: AANAT1lo mutants have increased recovery sleep following deprivation.
source: In Drosophila, mutants of arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase 1 (AANAT1lo) were reported to have normal baseline amounts of sleep and motor activity, but increased recovery sleep ('rebound') following deprivation (Shaw et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shaw et al., 2000.

claim: AANAT1 corresponds to speck, a long-known mutation characterized by a darkly pigmented region at the wing hinge.
source: AANAT1 corresponds to speck, a long-known mutation characterized by a darkly pigmented region at the wing hinge (Spana et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Spana et al., 2020.

claim: AANAT1 can acetylate and inactivate monoamines in vitro.
source: AANAT1 can acetylate and inactivate monoamines in vitro (Hintermann et al., 1995), but the role of AANAT1 in vivo remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hintermann et al., 1995.

claim: The role of AANAT1 in vivo remains poorly understood.
source: AANAT1 can acetylate and inactivate monoamines in vitro (Hintermann et al., 1995), but the role of AANAT1 in vivo remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: AANAT1 levels in astrocytes first rise then decline markedly overnight.
source: We report here that AANAT1 is expressed in astrocytes and subsets of neurons in the adult Drosophila brain, with levels in astrocytes first rising then declining markedly overnight.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing AANAT1 levels at different time points during the dark period.

claim: In sleep deprived AANAT1 mutant flies, heightened recovery sleep is accompanied by increased serotonin and dopamine levels in the brain.
source: In sleep deprived AANAT1 mutant flies, heightened recovery sleep is accompanied by increased serotonin and dopamine levels in the brain.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-MS measurements and sleep monitoring data.

claim: AANAT1 functions in astrocytes to limit the amount of recovery sleep that flies take in response to sleep deprivation.
source: With cell type selective AANAT1 knockdown, we find that AANAT1 functions in astrocytes, but not neurons, to limit the amount of recovery sleep that flies take in response to sleep deprivation (SD).
evidence: This is supported by cell-type specific RNAi knockdown experiments and sleep monitoring data.

claim: AANAT1 does not function in neurons to limit the amount of recovery sleep that flies take in response to sleep deprivation.
source: With cell type selective AANAT1 knockdown, we find that AANAT1 functions in astrocytes, but not neurons, to limit the amount of recovery sleep that flies take in response to sleep deprivation (SD).
evidence: This is supported by neuron-specific RNAi knockdown experiments and sleep monitoring data.

claim: Astrocytes play a crucial role in the regulation of monoamine bioavailability and homeostatic sleep drive.
source: These findings identify a critical role for astrocytes in the regulation of monoamine bioavailability and calibration of the response to sleep need.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: AANAT1 immunoreactivity was observed in the cytoplasm of many cells in the embryonic central nervous system.
source: AANAT1 immunoreactivity was observed in the cytoplasm of many cells (Figure 1A) but was absent in age-matched ventral nerve cords of embryos that were homozygous for a deletion of the entire AANAT1 gene (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: AANAT1 immunoreactivity was absent in age-matched ventral nerve cords of embryos that were homozygous for a deletion of the entire AANAT1 gene.
source: AANAT1 immunoreactivity was observed in the cytoplasm of many cells (Figure 1A) but was absent in age-matched ventral nerve cords of embryos that were homozygous for a deletion of the entire AANAT1 gene (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B, confirming antibody specificity.

claim: AANAT1 was present in distinct populations of cells throughout the adult brain.
source: In adult brains co-immunostained with anti-Bruchpilot (nc82, Figure 1C), a presynaptic marker that labels neuropil regions, AANAT1 was present in distinct populations of cells throughout the brain.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AANAT1 was expressed in sub-populations of neurons throughout the brain.
source: We found that AANAT1 was expressed in sub-populations of neurons (anti-Elav positive (+), Figure 1D,D') and glia (anti-Repo+, Figure 1E,E') throughout the brain.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1D,D'.

claim: AANAT1 was expressed in sub-populations of glia throughout the brain.
source: We found that AANAT1 was expressed in sub-populations of neurons (anti-Elav positive (+), Figure 1D,D') and glia (anti-Repo+, Figure 1E,E') throughout the brain.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E,E'.

claim: In glial cells AANAT1 was primarily cytoplasmic.
source: In glial cells AANAT1 was primarily cytoplasmic, but in neurons AANAT1 often appeared to localize to the nucleus.
evidence: This is based on observations from immunohistochemistry data.

claim: In neurons AANAT1 often appeared to localize to the nucleus.
source: In glial cells AANAT1 was primarily cytoplasmic, but in neurons AANAT1 often appeared to localize to the nucleus.
evidence: This is based on observations from immunohistochemistry data.

claim: All AANAT1-positive glial cells in the central brain are astrocytes.
source: With the astrocyte-specific Alrm-Gal4 driving expression of a Red Fluorescent Protein (RFP) reporter (Alrm >nuRFP), we confirmed that all AANAT1-positive glial cells in the central brain are astrocytes (Figure 1F–F'').
evidence: This is supported by co-labeling experiments shown in Figure 1F-F''.

claim: Only a subset of astrocytes in the optic lobes that reside between the medulla and lobula did not express AANAT1.
source: Only a subset of astrocytes in the optic lobes that reside between the medulla and lobula did not express AANAT1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AANAT1 could be observed in the thin, neuropil-infiltrating processes of astrocytes.
source: With RNA interference (RNAi)-mediated knockdown of AANAT1 from all neurons using the driver nSyb-Gal4, the AANAT1-positive glial cells in the central brain could be identified more clearly as astrocytes by their ramified morphology, where AANAT1 could be observed in their thin, neuropil-infiltrating processes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,G,H).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,G,H.

claim: AANAT1 expression was absent from ensheathing glia marked by R56F03-Gal4.
source: In contrast to astrocytes, AANAT1 expression was absent from ensheathing glia marked by R56F03-Gal4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: AANAT1 is expressed in an average of 14.5 ± 4.8 of 60 ± 3.4 (25%) of serotonergic cells labeled with Trh >mCD8 GFP.
source: AANAT1 was expressed in an average of 14.5 ± 4.8 of 60 ± 3.4 (25%) of serotonergic cells labeled with Trh >mCD8 GFP (Figure 1H,I–I'',N), which were found largely in a cluster within the medial subeosophageal ganglion (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: AANAT1-expressing serotonergic cells were found largely in a cluster within the medial subeosophageal ganglion.
source: AANAT1 was expressed in an average of 14.5 ± 4.8 of 60 ± 3.4 (25%) of serotonergic cells labeled with Trh >mCD8 GFP (Figure 1H,I–I'',N), which were found largely in a cluster within the medial subeosophageal ganglion (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: AANAT1 did not co-label cells expressing TH >mCD8 GFP or Tdc2 >mCD8 GFP.
source: However, AANAT1 did not co-label cells expressing TH >mCD8 GFP or Tdc2 >mCD8 GFP (Figure 1J,K–K'', L,M–M'', N), indicating AANAT1 is not expressed in dopaminergic or octopaminergic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1J,K-K'', L,M-M'', N.

claim: AANAT1 is not expressed in dopaminergic or octopaminergic neurons.
source: However, AANAT1 did not co-label cells expressing TH >mCD8 GFP or Tdc2 >mCD8 GFP (Figure 1J,K–K'', L,M–M'', N), indicating AANAT1 is not expressed in dopaminergic or octopaminergic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1J,K-K'', L,M-M'', N.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing data shows AANAT1 transcripts in astrocytes and serotonergic neurons.
source: These results are corroborated by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing AANAT1 transcripts in astrocytes and serotonergic neurons (Croset et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Croset et al., 2018.

claim: AANAT1 is present in sub-populations of neurons that release glutamate, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), or acetylcholine.
source: To identify the other types of neurons expressing AANAT1, we used a mCD8-GFP reporter driven by either MiMIC-vGlut, Gad1-Gal4, or Cha-Gal4 and found AANAT1 in sub-populations of neurons that release glutamate, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), or acetylcholine, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1R-W'').
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1R-W''.

claim: Monoamines are mainly synthesized in the neurons that release them.
source: Monoamines are mainly synthesized in the neurons that release them, and it is generally understood that their re-uptake into these same neurons occurs via specific transport proteins to prevent their accumulation at synapses (Martin and Krantz, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation to Martin and Krantz, 2014.

claim: Re-uptake of monoamines into neurons occurs via specific transport proteins to prevent their accumulation at synapses.
source: Monoamines are mainly synthesized in the neurons that release them, and it is generally understood that their re-uptake into these same neurons occurs via specific transport proteins to prevent their accumulation at synapses (Martin and Krantz, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation to Martin and Krantz, 2014.

claim: Cells that produce and release monoamines do not necessarily contribute to their catabolism via AANAT1.
source: Absence of AANAT1 from dopaminergic or octopaminergic neurons showed that cells that produce and release monoamines do not necessarily contribute to their catabolism via AANAT1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AANAT1 is not expressed in dopaminergic or octopaminergic neurons.

claim: Non-monoaminergic neurons (glutamatergic, GABAergic, and cholinergic) could contribute to regulation of monoamine bioavailability in the brain along with astrocytes.
source: However, the presence of AANAT1 in subsets of glutamatergic, GABAergic and cholinergic neurons suggests that, along with astrocytes, these non-monoaminergic neurons could contribute to regulation of monoamine bioavailability in the brain.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AANAT1 is expressed in these neuron types.

claim: The AANAT1 gene produces two protein isoforms.
source: The AANAT1 gene produces two protein isoforms, the shorter of which (FlyBase AANAT1-PA, 240aa in length), previously known as aaNAT1b, is more predominant (Brodbeck et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brodbeck et al., 1998.

claim: The shorter AANAT1 isoform (FlyBase AANAT1-PA, 240aa in length) is more predominant.
source: The AANAT1 gene produces two protein isoforms, the shorter of which (FlyBase AANAT1-PA, 240aa in length), previously known as aaNAT1b, is more predominant (Brodbeck et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brodbeck et al., 1998.

claim: The shorter AANAT1 isoform was observed to be lost in AANAT1lo mutants.
source: This shorter isoform was observed to be lost in AANAT1lo mutants (Hintermann et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hintermann et al., 1996.

claim: AANAT1lo is a spontaneous mutation that arose from insertion of a transposable element into the AANAT1 gene.
source: AANAT1lo is a spontaneous mutation that arose from insertion of a transposable element into the AANAT1 gene, and tissue extracts from these flies have reduced AANAT1 activity (Hintermann et al., 1996; Maranda and Hodgetts, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hintermann et al., 1996 and Maranda and Hodgetts, 1977.

claim: Tissue extracts from AANAT1lo flies have reduced AANAT1 activity.
source: AANAT1lo is a spontaneous mutation that arose from insertion of a transposable element into the AANAT1 gene, and tissue extracts from these flies have reduced AANAT1 activity (Hintermann et al., 1996; Maranda and Hodgetts, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hintermann et al., 1996 and Maranda and Hodgetts, 1977.

claim: Only the shorter AANAT1 isoform was observed in control brain extracts by western blotting.
source: Using our new AANAT1 antiserum to perform western blotting of brain extracts, we observed only the shorter isoform in controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In AANAT1lo homozygotes, AANAT1 protein levels were reduced to 13% of iso31 controls.
source: In AANAT1lo homozygotes and hemizygotes (AANAT1lo/In(2LR)Px[4]), AANAT1 protein levels were reduced to 13 and 8% of iso31 controls, respectively (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot quantification shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: In AANAT1lo hemizygotes (AANAT1lo/In(2LR)Px[4]), AANAT1 protein levels were reduced to 8% of iso31 controls.
source: In AANAT1lo homozygotes and hemizygotes (AANAT1lo/In(2LR)Px[4]), AANAT1 protein levels were reduced to 13 and 8% of iso31 controls, respectively (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot quantification shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: In AANAT1lo flies, there is residual AANAT1 expression in some Elav+ neurons.
source: This was confirmed with IHC in the brains of AANAT1lo flies (Figure 2C–E), where we noted residual AANAT1 expression in some Elav+ neurons, but complete loss of AANAT1 from astrocytes (Figure 2F–F', G–G').
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2F-F', G-G'.

claim: In AANAT1lo flies, there is complete loss of AANAT1 from astrocytes.
source: This was confirmed with IHC in the brains of AANAT1lo flies (Figure 2C–E), where we noted residual AANAT1 expression in some Elav+ neurons, but complete loss of AANAT1 from astrocytes (Figure 2F–F', G–G').
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2F-F', G-G'.

claim: Serotonin and dopamine are substrates for AANAT1 with similar affinities in vitro.
source: In vitro studies have shown that serotonin and dopamine are substrates for AANAT1 with similar affinities (Hintermann et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hintermann et al., 1995.

claim: Under baseline sleep-cycle conditions, serotonin and dopamine levels in AANAT1lo flies were similar to controls.
source: Under baseline sleep-cycle conditions, where brain tissues were collected in a 3 hr window after lights-ON (ZT0), serotonin and dopamine levels in AANAT1lo flies were similar to controls (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-MS measurements shown in Figure 2I.

claim: After 12 hr of overnight sleep deprivation, AANAT1lo brains had a robust increase in the levels of serotonin and dopamine compared to controls.
source: However, if this window was preceded by 12 hr (ZT12-ZT24) of SD overnight, AANAT1lo brains had a robust increase in the levels of serotonin and dopamine compared to controls (Figure 2I), but this had no effect on octopamine levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-MS measurements shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Sleep deprivation had no effect on octopamine levels in AANAT1lo flies.
source: However, if this window was preceded by 12 hr (ZT12-ZT24) of SD overnight, AANAT1lo brains had a robust increase in the levels of serotonin and dopamine compared to controls (Figure 2I), but this had no effect on octopamine levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-MS measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In control animals, the sleep deprivation protocol did not affect the levels of measured monoamines.
source: Importantly, in control animals the SD protocol itself did not appear to affect the levels of measured monoamines, or of AANAT1 itself (Figure 2J,K).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-MS measurements and western blot data shown in Figure 2J,K.

claim: In control animals, the sleep deprivation protocol did not affect the levels of AANAT1 itself.
source: Importantly, in control animals the SD protocol itself did not appear to affect the levels of measured monoamines, or of AANAT1 itself (Figure 2J,K).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2J,K.

claim: Sleep deprivation did not change the levels of Ebony in AANAT1lo flies.
source: Further, we did not observe changes in the levels of another monoamine catabolic enzyme known to be expressed in astrocytes (Ebony) in either AANAT1lo flies, or in flies subjected to SD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: Sleep deprivation did not change the levels of Ebony in flies subjected to SD.
source: Further, we did not observe changes in the levels of another monoamine catabolic enzyme known to be expressed in astrocytes (Ebony) in either AANAT1lo flies, or in flies subjected to SD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: Catabolism of serotonin and dopamine in the brains of flies lacking AANAT1 is severely compromised upon sleep deprivation.
source: We conclude that catabolism of serotonin and dopamine in the brains of flies lacking AANAT1 is severely compromised upon SD, leading to inappropriate accumulation of these monoamines.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HPLC-MS data showing increased monoamine levels in AANAT1 mutants after sleep deprivation.

claim: Loss of AANAT1 leads to inappropriate accumulation of serotonin and dopamine upon sleep deprivation.
source: We conclude that catabolism of serotonin and dopamine in the brains of flies lacking AANAT1 is severely compromised upon SD, leading to inappropriate accumulation of these monoamines.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HPLC-MS data showing increased monoamine levels in AANAT1 mutants after sleep deprivation.

claim: AANAT1lo flies have normal motor activity.
source: The AANAT1lo mutation increases homeostatic sleep following deprivation (Shaw et al., 2000), suggesting AANAT1 could be key to how the brain limits the homeostatic response to sleep need. AANAT1lo is also interesting because these flies were reported to have normal motor activity, and intact daily patterns of sleep (Shaw et al., 2000), allowing genetic dissection of homeostatic sleep- control independent of the regulation of baseline sleep.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shaw et al., 2000.

claim: AANAT1lo flies have intact daily patterns of sleep.
source: The AANAT1lo mutation increases homeostatic sleep following deprivation (Shaw et al., 2000), suggesting AANAT1 could be key to how the brain limits the homeostatic response to sleep need. AANAT1lo is also interesting because these flies were reported to have normal motor activity, and intact daily patterns of sleep (Shaw et al., 2000), allowing genetic dissection of homeostatic sleep- control independent of the regulation of baseline sleep.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shaw et al., 2000.

claim: AANAT1lo allows genetic dissection of homeostatic sleep-control independent of the regulation of baseline sleep.
source: The AANAT1lo mutation increases homeostatic sleep following deprivation (Shaw et al., 2000), suggesting AANAT1 could be key to how the brain limits the homeostatic response to sleep need. AANAT1lo is also interesting because these flies were reported to have normal motor activity, and intact daily patterns of sleep (Shaw et al., 2000), allowing genetic dissection of homeostatic sleep- control independent of the regulation of baseline sleep.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AANAT1lo affects homeostatic sleep but not baseline sleep.

claim: Knockdown of AANAT1 in neurons with nSyb-Gal4 resulted in normal patterns of baseline sleep.
source: Knockdown of AANAT1 in neurons with either line resulted in normal patterns of baseline sleep (Figure 3A–H), as reported for the AANAT1lo allele (Shaw et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 3A-H.

claim: Flies with neuronal AANAT1 knockdown had lower levels of activity than controls while awake during daytime.
source: While awake during daytime, these animals had lower levels of activity than controls carrying either the GAL4 or UAS transgene alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), but their total daytime sleep amount was similar to at least one of the controls (Figure 3B,F), as were the length of daytime sleep bouts (Figure 3C,G) and their number (Figure 3D,H).
evidence: This is supported by activity index data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Flies with neuronal AANAT1 knockdown had total daytime sleep amount similar to at least one of the controls.
source: While awake during daytime, these animals had lower levels of activity than controls carrying either the GAL4 or UAS transgene alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), but their total daytime sleep amount was similar to at least one of the controls (Figure 3B,F), as were the length of daytime sleep bouts (Figure 3C,G) and their number (Figure 3D,H).
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 3B,F.

claim: One RNAi line (AANAT-RNAi 2, JF02142) led to increased amount of nighttime sleep when used for neuronal knockdown.
source: When we examined the amount of nighttime sleep compared to controls, we found that one RNAi line (AANAT-RNAi 2, JF02142), but not the other (AANAT-RNAi 1, HMS01617), led to increased amount of nighttime sleep (Figure 3B,F).
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 3B,F.

claim: For knockdown with AANAT-RNAi 2 in neurons, sleep bouts during the night were increased in duration and decreased in number, suggesting improved sleep consolidation at night.
source: For knockdown with this RNAi line only, sleep bouts during the night were increased in duration and decreased in number, suggesting improved sleep consolidation at night (Figure 3C–D;G-H).
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 3C-D, G-H.

claim: Flies with neuronal AANAT1 knockdown (nSyb >AANAT1 RNAi) did not display enhanced recovery sleep after sleep deprivation.
source: We then assessed whether AANAT1 knockdown in neurons (nSyb >AANAT1 RNAi) would impact sleep recovery after SD, as was observed in AANAT1lo flies. For this, flies were subjected to overnight mechanical SD and we found, somewhat surprisingly, that these flies did not display enhanced recovery sleep the next day (Figure 3I–L).
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 3I-L.

claim: Astrocyte-selective AANAT1 knockdown (Alrm >AANAT1 RNAi) had no effect on the numbers of astrocytes present in the brain.
source: Next, we used Alrm-Gal4 to selectively deplete AANAT1 expression from astrocytes with RNAi (Alrm >AANAT1 RNAi). This had no effect on the numbers of astrocytes present in the brain (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Flies with astrocyte-selective AANAT1 knockdown showed normal baseline patterns and amounts of daytime and nighttime sleep compared to controls.
source: These flies showed normal baseline patterns and amounts of daytime and nighttime sleep compared to controls (Figure 4B–E), but while awake they were less active than controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 4B-E.

claim: Flies with astrocyte-selective AANAT1 knockdown were less active than controls while awake.
source: These flies showed normal baseline patterns and amounts of daytime and nighttime sleep compared to controls (Figure 4B–E), but while awake they were less active than controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by activity index data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Upon overnight mechanical sleep deprivation, flies with astrocyte-selective AANAT1 knockdown had increased recovery sleep the next day.
source: However, upon overnight mechanical SD, these flies had increased recovery sleep the next day (Figure 4F–I), mimicking AANAT1lo flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 4F-I.

claim: Flies with astrocyte-selective AANAT1 knockdown mimic AANAT1lo flies in their recovery sleep response.
source: However, upon overnight mechanical SD, these flies had increased recovery sleep the next day (Figure 4F–I), mimicking AANAT1lo flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 4F-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: AANAT1 overexpression in astrocytes increased recovery sleep following deprivation.
source: Like AANAT1 loss-of-function, AANAT1 overexpression in astrocytes also increased recovery sleep following deprivation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), underscoring the importance of regulated astrocytic AANAT1 levels in sleep homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Regulated astrocytic AANAT1 levels are important in sleep homeostasis.
source: Like AANAT1 loss-of-function, AANAT1 overexpression in astrocytes also increased recovery sleep following deprivation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), underscoring the importance of regulated astrocytic AANAT1 levels in sleep homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both loss and overexpression of AANAT1 in astrocytes affect recovery sleep.

claim: Astrocyte-selective AANAT1 knockdown led to increased levels of brain serotonin and dopamine after sleep deprivation in most samples compared to controls.
source: With HPLC-MS, we noted that astrocyte-selective AANAT1 knockdown led to increased levels of brain serotonin and dopamine after SD in most samples compared to controls (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-MS measurements shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The increase in serotonin and dopamine levels after astrocyte-selective AANAT1 knockdown did not reach statistical significance.
source: This did not reach statistical significance however, perhaps because of an outlier in each of the control groups, or perhaps because AANAT1 knockdown in astrocytes affects the levels of only a portion of serotonin and dopamine in the brain, albeit an important portion with respect to sleep homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the text discussing the HPLC-MS results.

claim: Drosophila astrocytes employ AANAT1 to limit accumulation of serotonin and dopamine upon sleep deprivation.
source: Together with the clear increases seen in AANAT1lo flies (Figure 2I), these data suggest that Drosophila astrocytes employ AANAT1 to limit accumulation of serotonin and dopamine upon SD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined HPLC-MS data from AANAT1lo flies and astrocyte-selective knockdown experiments.

claim: Loss of AANAT1 does not affect astrocyte numbers or their terminal differentiation.
source: Since loss of AANAT1 does not affect astrocyte numbers or their terminal differentiation, we think it unlikely to play a developmental role and favor the idea that AANAT1 functions in mature astrocytes to limit recovery sleep.
evidence: This is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: AANAT1 is unlikely to play a developmental role in astrocytes.
source: Since loss of AANAT1 does not affect astrocyte numbers or their terminal differentiation, we think it unlikely to play a developmental role and favor the idea that AANAT1 functions in mature astrocytes to limit recovery sleep.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AANAT1 loss does not affect astrocyte numbers or differentiation.

claim: AANAT1 functions in mature astrocytes to limit recovery sleep.
source: Since loss of AANAT1 does not affect astrocyte numbers or their terminal differentiation, we think it unlikely to play a developmental role and favor the idea that AANAT1 functions in mature astrocytes to limit recovery sleep.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental findings.

claim: During the dark phase, most astrocytes throughout the brain showed obvious changes of AANAT1 levels.
source: Interestingly, during the dark phase most astrocytes throughout the brain showed obvious changes of AANAT1 levels.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry observations at different time points.

claim: Dark period AANAT1 expression in astrocyte cell bodies peaked at ZT15.
source: Dark period AANAT1 expression in astrocyte cell bodies peaked at ZT15, declined markedly to undetectable levels by ZT21 (Figure 4K), and was re-established at lights-ON (ZT24).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of AANAT1 levels at different time points shown in Figure 4K.

claim: AANAT1 expression in astrocyte cell bodies declined markedly to undetectable levels by ZT21.
source: Dark period AANAT1 expression in astrocyte cell bodies peaked at ZT15, declined markedly to undetectable levels by ZT21 (Figure 4K), and was re-established at lights-ON (ZT24).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of AANAT1 levels at different time points shown in Figure 4K.

claim: AANAT1 expression in astrocyte cell bodies was re-established at lights-ON (ZT24).
source: Dark period AANAT1 expression in astrocyte cell bodies peaked at ZT15, declined markedly to undetectable levels by ZT21 (Figure 4K), and was re-established at lights-ON (ZT24).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of AANAT1 levels at different time points shown in Figure 4K.

claim: AANAT1 is expressed in astrocytes that reside throughout the brain.
source: AANAT1 is expressed in astrocytes that reside throughout the brain, and so it remains unclear whether it modulates sleep homeostasis by acting within a particular region of the brain, or more broadly.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry observations throughout the brain.

claim: It remains unclear whether AANAT1 modulates sleep homeostasis by acting within a particular region of the brain, or more broadly.
source: AANAT1 is expressed in astrocytes that reside throughout the brain, and so it remains unclear whether it modulates sleep homeostasis by acting within a particular region of the brain, or more broadly.
evidence: This is stated as an open question in the discussion.

claim: The neuropils of key sleep centers (MB, EB and FSB) had no AANAT1 staining from infiltrative astrocytes.
source: Interestingly, the neuropils of key sleep centers (MB, EB and FSB; Figure 1—figure supplement 1K–Q) had no AANAT1 staining from infiltrative astrocytes, raising the likelihood it acts elsewhere.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K-Q.

claim: AANAT1 likely acts outside of key sleep centers (MB, EB and FSB).
source: Interestingly, the neuropils of key sleep centers (MB, EB and FSB; Figure 1—figure supplement 1K–Q) had no AANAT1 staining from infiltrative astrocytes, raising the likelihood it acts elsewhere.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AANAT1 is absent from astrocytes in these sleep centers.

claim: It remains to be established whether the effect of AANAT1 on sleep homeostasis is due to serotonin, dopamine, or both.
source: Finally, it remains to be established whether the effect of AANAT1 on sleep homeostasis is due to serotonin, dopamine, or both.
evidence: This is stated as an open question in the discussion.

claim: In Drosophila, serotonergic signaling in the brain promotes sleep.
source: In Drosophila, serotonergic signaling in the brain promotes sleep, while dopaminergic signaling promotes waking.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of Drosophila sleep research.

claim: In Drosophila, dopaminergic signaling promotes waking.
source: In Drosophila, serotonergic signaling in the brain promotes sleep, while dopaminergic signaling promotes waking.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of Drosophila sleep research.

claim: Levels of both serotonin and dopamine are upregulated in AANAT1lo mutants upon sleep deprivation, where increased sleep prevails.
source: Levels of both serotonin and dopamine are upregulated in AANAT1lo mutants upon SD, where increased sleep prevails.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-MS measurements and sleep monitoring data.

claim: AANAT1 could act in astrocytes to limit the deprivation-dependent accumulation of sleep-promoting serotonin.
source: It stands to reason that AANAT1 could act in astrocytes to limit the deprivation-dependent accumulation of sleep-promoting serotonin.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Thermogenetic activation of wake-promoting dopaminergic neurons at night promotes compensatory sleep the next day.
source: It is also possible that dopamine accumulation plays a role, since thermogenetic activation of wake-promoting dopaminergic neurons at night promotes compensatory sleep the next day.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Wake-promoting dopaminergic neurons are upstream of circuits that produce homeostatic responses to extended wakefulness.
source: This suggests these particular neurons are upstream of circuits that produce homeostatic responses to extended wakefulness (Dubowy and Sehgal, 2017; Seidner et al., 2015), and astrocytic AANAT1 could somehow restrict dopaminergic signaling from these neurons overnight.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dubowy and Sehgal, 2017 and Seidner et al., 2015.

claim: Astrocytic AANAT1 could restrict dopaminergic signaling from wake-promoting neurons overnight.
source: This suggests these particular neurons are upstream of circuits that produce homeostatic responses to extended wakefulness (Dubowy and Sehgal, 2017; Seidner et al., 2015), and astrocytic AANAT1 could somehow restrict dopaminergic signaling from these neurons overnight.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings and previous knowledge.

claim: Astrocytes are specifically engaged to catabolize monoamines whose levels are elevated by overnight sleep deprivation.
source: Our findings illustrate a newly discovered role for astrocytes in the control of monoamine bioavailability and homeostatic sleep drive, where they are specifically engaged to catabolize monoamines whose levels are elevated by overnight SD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental findings.

claim: Drosophila astrocytes express the enzyme Ebony, which couples dopamine to N-β-alanine.
source: Drosophila astrocytes also express the enzyme Ebony, which couples dopamine to N-β-alanine (Suh and Jackson, 2007), and a receptor for octopamine and tyramine (Ma et al., 2016), reinforcing how they are well-equipped to metabolize monoamines, and to monitor and respond to monoaminergic neuronal activity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Suh and Jackson, 2007.

claim: Drosophila astrocytes express a receptor for octopamine and tyramine.
source: Drosophila astrocytes also express the enzyme Ebony, which couples dopamine to N-β-alanine (Suh and Jackson, 2007), and a receptor for octopamine and tyramine (Ma et al., 2016), reinforcing how they are well-equipped to metabolize monoamines, and to monitor and respond to monoaminergic neuronal activity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ma et al., 2016.

claim: Drosophila astrocytes are well-equipped to metabolize monoamines, and to monitor and respond to monoaminergic neuronal activity.
source: Drosophila astrocytes also express the enzyme Ebony, which couples dopamine to N-β-alanine (Suh and Jackson, 2007), and a receptor for octopamine and tyramine (Ma et al., 2016), reinforcing how they are well-equipped to metabolize monoamines, and to monitor and respond to monoaminergic neuronal activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of multiple monoamine-related enzymes and receptors in astrocytes.

claim: Gene expression studies and RNA sequencing databases do not provide evidence for monoamine-synthesizing enzymes in Drosophila astrocytes.
source: Neither gene expression studies nor RNA sequencing databases provide evidence for monoamine-synthesizing enzymes in Drosophila astrocytes, so it appears likely that monoamines inactivated by AANAT1 in astrocytes are brought into these cells by an unidentified transporter.
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene expression studies and RNA sequencing databases.

claim: Monoamines inactivated by AANAT1 in astrocytes are likely brought into these cells by an unidentified transporter.
source: Neither gene expression studies nor RNA sequencing databases provide evidence for monoamine-synthesizing enzymes in Drosophila astrocytes, so it appears likely that monoamines inactivated by AANAT1 in astrocytes are brought into these cells by an unidentified transporter.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of monoamine-synthesizing enzymes in astrocytes.

claim: Astrocytes are particularly well-suited for regulating sleep because they have ramified processes that infiltrate neuropil regions to lie in close proximity to synapses.
source: Astrocytes are particularly well-suited for regulating sleep in this way because they have ramified processes that infiltrate neuropil regions to lie in close proximity to synapses.
evidence: This is based on the known morphology of astrocytes.

claim: Sleep deprivation can reduce the degree of contact between astrocytes and neurons in the fly brain.
source: SD can seemingly reduce the degree of contact between astrocytes and neurons in the fly brain (Vanderheyden et al., 2019), and so it is possible that these structural changes could influence monoamine uptake and inactivation by astrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vanderheyden et al., 2019.

claim: Structural changes between astrocytes and neurons during sleep deprivation could influence monoamine uptake and inactivation by astrocytes.
source: SD can seemingly reduce the degree of contact between astrocytes and neurons in the fly brain (Vanderheyden et al., 2019), and so it is possible that these structural changes could influence monoamine uptake and inactivation by astrocytes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on previous findings.

claim: In neurons, AANAT1 may function to limit sleep consolidation at night.
source: In neurons, AANAT1 may function to limit sleep consolidation at night, but evidence for this came from only one of the two RNAi lines used in this study and was not observed in AANAT1lo mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a speculation based on data from one RNAi line.

claim: Evidence for AANAT1 limiting sleep consolidation at night came from only one of the two RNAi lines used in this study.
source: In neurons, AANAT1 may function to limit sleep consolidation at night, but evidence for this came from only one of the two RNAi lines used in this study and was not observed in AANAT1lo mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: Loss of the related enzyme aanat2 in zebrafish larvae decreases baseline sleep.
source: In light of this, we note that loss of the related enzyme aanat2 in zebrafish larvae decreases baseline sleep (Gandhi et al., 2015), which could be attributed to a loss of melatonin since the AANAT1 product N-acetylserotonin is an intermediate in the synthesis of melatonin in vertebrates (Hintermann et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gandhi et al., 2015.

claim: The AANAT1 product N-acetylserotonin is an intermediate in the synthesis of melatonin in vertebrates.
source: In light of this, we note that loss of the related enzyme aanat2 in zebrafish larvae decreases baseline sleep (Gandhi et al., 2015), which could be attributed to a loss of melatonin since the AANAT1 product N-acetylserotonin is an intermediate in the synthesis of melatonin in vertebrates (Hintermann et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hintermann et al., 1996.

claim: The appropriate balance and cellular context of AANAT activity is critical for the regulation of sleep.
source: Clearly, the appropriate balance and cellular context of AANAT activity is critical for the regulation of sleep, and we show here in Drosophila that astrocytes are an important contributor to this balance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental findings.

claim: Astrocytes in rodents express monoamine transporters and receptors for dopamine and serotonin.
source: Interestingly, astrocytes in rodents express the monoamine transporters and receptors for dopamine and serotonin (Bacq et al., 2012; Baganz et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2012; Petrelli et al., 2020; Sandén et al., 2000; Vaarmann et al., 2010), raising the possibility that astrocytes in mammals might also participate in mechanisms of sleep regulation involving monoaminergic neural signaling.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Astrocytes in mammals might participate in mechanisms of sleep regulation involving monoaminergic neural signaling.
source: Interestingly, astrocytes in rodents express the monoamine transporters and receptors for dopamine and serotonin (Bacq et al., 2012; Baganz et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2012; Petrelli et al., 2020; Sandén et al., 2000; Vaarmann et al., 2010), raising the possibility that astrocytes in mammals might also participate in mechanisms of sleep regulation involving monoaminergic neural signaling.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings in Drosophila and the expression of monoamine-related proteins in mammalian astrocytes.

claim: AANAT1 was weakly expressed in only a few astrocytes at 48 hr after puparium formation (APF).
source: We characterized AANAT1 expression in astrocytes during pupal development with immunochemistry, and found AANAT1 to be expressed weakly in only a few astrocytes at 48 hr after puparium formation (APF), then gradually more strongly in most but not all astrocytes at 72 hr and 96 hr APF (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-I'').
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-I''.

claim: AANAT1 was expressed gradually more strongly in most but not all astrocytes at 72 hr and 96 hr APF.
source: We characterized AANAT1 expression in astrocytes during pupal development with immunochemistry, and found AANAT1 to be expressed weakly in only a few astrocytes at 48 hr after puparium formation (APF), then gradually more strongly in most but not all astrocytes at 72 hr and 96 hr APF (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-I'').
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-I''.

claim: Adult flies with AANAT1 knockdown in glia using the TARGET system showed increased recovery sleep compared to the UAS control but not the Gal4 control.
source: When adult flies were raised at 32°C to deplete AANAT1 from glia using RNAi, these animals showed increased recovery sleep compared to the UAS control but not the Gal4 control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J-K).
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J-K.
